name: Dinebra
look_here_first: MUCRONATE SPRANGLETOP (subsp. mucronata) — annual with many slender ascending branches along a central axis and 2–4(-5)-flowered tiny spikelets. Short truncate/irregular membranous true ligule and raised-base sheath hairs must be inspected on the target itself. Four Central Texas Bob Harms comparison images show DIFFERENT subspecies brachiata, not a confirmed mucronata; the two separately labelled native green sprangletop photographs show larger multi-flowered units. Do not equate species complex or background other subspecies with target.

recognition.where_to_look_first: MUCRONATE SPRANGLETOP — think FINE-BRANCHED ANNUAL: an often slender warm-season annual with NUMEROUS almost straight ascending flowering branches scattered along a main axis, like a narrow brush. Check a mature tiny spikelet with 10–20×: typically 2–4 florets in a ca. 2–4 mm laterally flattened spikelet; short glumes and a tiny pointed glume tip (mucro) require a lens, and do NOT by themselves prove subspecies. Look at the leaf sheath for distinct bulbous/papillose-based spreading hairs and examine the true membranous ligule. The existing source photograph shows only broad panicle/leaf features: it cannot certify floret number, sheath-hair bases, glume mucro or mucronata versus other D. panicea subspecies.
priority: Entire annual fibrous-rooted base and full many-branched slender head
Under 10–20× measure one short spikelet and count 2–4 florets
Photograph bulbous-based spreading sheath hairs and true membrane ligule separately
For subsp. mucronata obtain authenticated morphology separating subsp. brachiata
recognition.warning: One overall field photograph does not substantiate fine glume point, floret number or a precise subspecies identity.

comparison_lesson.title: Dinebra mucronate sprangletop versus green sprangletop and lovegrasses
comparison_lesson.memory_rule: MANY THIN BRANCHES + ANNUAL BASE + TINY USUALLY 2–4-FLORET SPIKELETS suggests Dinebra panicea. Subspecies mucronata needs close botanical determination, not an ordinary photo.
quick_split: GREEN SPRANGLETOP / Disakisperma dubium: generally a larger perennial arising from a lasting base, commonly with fewer longer near-fingerlike branches, and larger 4–12 mm spikelets containing about 4–13 florets. MUCRONATE SPRANGLETOP / Dinebra panicea subsp. mucronata: slender ANNUAL with many ascending slender branches, generally much smaller ~2–4 mm spikelets with ~2–4 florets and often bulbous-based sheath hairs. Counts can overlap at 4 florets, so a single spikelet count isn't decisive. ERAGROSTIS lovegrasses: many have an airy panicle too but individual spikelets have several fertile florets in overlapping ranks, and the branching/spikelet anatomy differs. Within DINEBRA, the other subspecies of D. panicea can look extremely similar; a photograph labeled merely Dinebra panicea is NOT independently sufficient to certify subsp. mucronata. Old Leptochloa mucronata refers to this taxon in the Kew treatment; Leptochloa filiformis and other older names have been applied differently in historical treatments.
comparison_lesson.guardrail: Only D. panicea subsp. mucronata is installed. Never create a duplicate for Leptochloa mucronata, and do not treat a species-level macro as subspecies-certified.

what_to_teach_crew: Start at the fine many-branched inflorescence, not the common name 'sprangletop'.
Find true annual rooting and compare with perennial Disakisperma.
Count FLORETS WITHIN ONE tiny spikelet under 10–20× and measure the spikelet; never use branch count alone.
Examine upper glume mucro, papillose sheath hair bases and inner membrane ligule separately.
Distinguish field-level species complex from unproven subspecies; photograph voucher micros.
Remember Leptochloa mucronata synonym but no duplicate canonical card.
With Dinebra, a tiny MUCRONATE glume tip is a short point (often <1mm), NOT an obvious long awn. The plant's name alone does not prove the photo includes a visible mucro.
The public photo lesson uses BOB HARMS comparisons from DIFFERENT subsp. brachiata; the canonical target remains subsp. mucronata and is not photographically confirmed by those images.
Green sprangletop (Disakisperma dubium) is a different native perennial: compare its verified attached spikelets and multi-floret architecture, not seedhead shape alone.
visual_needs: FIRST: confirmed American/Texas DINEBRA PANICEA SUBSP. MUCRONATA small attached spikelet; distinguish BRAchiata comparison, 10-20x with 1mm scale.
SECOND: actual MUCRONATA 1-3mm truncate-erose true membranous ligule and papilla/bulbous hair base sheath detail with ruler.
THIRD: entire rooted annual mucronata, full many-branched narrow brushy flowering architecture.
FOURTH: matched brachiata photo/voucher at same scale plus caryopsis with or without ventral groove, actual glumes relative to florets.
Compare verified perennial green sprangletop Disakisperma dubium with much larger multiple-floret spikelets (two sourced local macro photos already in genus).
visual_status: FIELD_READY_PHOTO_GAPS — 4 REAL correctly named sibling subspecies brachiata macro photos newly archived, 2 actually documented native green sprangletop lookalike photos reused with 4 real existing arrows. Authentic mucronata macro, 1–3mm ligule, swollen sheath hair bases and tiny upper glume mucro still need source/voucher and scale.

comparison_matrix.title: Fine-branched sprangletop comparison
rows: Numerous fine branches, tiny ~2–4 mm spikelets usually 2–4 florets; confirm subspecies under microscope
Whole rooted plant and same-scale spikelets
Perennial, frequently fewer longer branches, larger ~4–12 mm and 4–13 florets
Lovegrass often airy panicle and multi-floreted spikelets; photo outline is unreliable alone

quick_field_id_tiles.heading: 01 · IS IT AN ANNUAL?
quick_field_id_tiles.short: Slender, fibrous-rooted grass; no lasting perennial crown
quick_field_id_tiles.details: Trace an attached plant downward. Mucronate sprangletop is an annual and can have culms bending at lower nodes. Native green sprangletop (Disakisperma dubium) normally has a robust persistent perennial base. A disconnected flowering branch doesn't prove lifespan.
quick_field_id_tiles.photo_status: ATTACHED TARGET ROOT/WHOLE PLANT NOT VERIFIED

quick_field_id_tiles.heading: 02 · FOLLOW THE FINGERS
quick_field_id_tiles.short: Many fine side racemes distributed along a long central axis
quick_field_id_tiles.details: The flower head can look like a narrow brush with numerous slender, nearly straight branches inserted at separate positions. The newly archived Bob Harms photographs are of the different subsp. brachiata; use them to learn shared architecture, NOT to confirm subsp. mucronata.

quick_field_id_tiles.heading: 03 · OPEN THE LEAF
quick_field_id_tiles.short: Check short membranous ligule AND raised-base sheath hairs
quick_field_id_tiles.details: NEW direct photo 190322lg by Jim Conrad from source-labelled ssp. mucronata visibly separates the whitish ragged membranous ligule at leaf blade/sheath junction from long white sheath hairs BELOW; both have explicit accurate broad arrows. This original lacks a ruler: do not infer measured ligule height or minute bulbous hair insertion.
quick_field_id_tiles.photo_status: TRUE source-verified MUCRONATA membranous ragged ligule and long SHEATH hairs photographed; original lacks 1-mm scale and individual papilla-base view

quick_field_id_tiles.heading: 04 · COUNT THE FLORETS
quick_field_id_tiles.short: Tiny multi-flowered spikelets; verify glume tips and pedicel
quick_field_id_tiles.details: A mature 2–4 mm Dinebra panicea complex spikelet often contains 2–4 florets. Under 20× follow the upper glume to its tiny mucro (short firm point), count REAL florets within one spikelet, and compare glumes against fertile florets. Subspecies separation requires mature glumes/fruit on correctly vouchered specimen; don't promote species-complex photo to exact mucronata.
quick_field_id_tiles.photo_status: Actual subspecies photographed with real mm ruler! Glume mucro not resolved; source from Yucatan not Hays.
